speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to add my support to the motion proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), a motion which goes to the root of many anxieties which plague so many Canadians at this time. If we do not decide now that positive action is called for, and if we do not then take decisive action, I am afraid the whole question of who is the prisoner and who is the jailer will be academic. We are on the verge today of losing sight of who it is who needs and deserves the protection of the law.
Things are so bad today, with respect to the prison system, that if it were not for the fact that people who are walking out of our prisons almost daily were not hardened criminals, the situation would be hilarious. In fact, in light of the unfavourable publicity being directed to the department of the Solicitor General I am surprised he even allows some of these people into jail! However, the situation is anything but hilarious when we consider that some of these people are murderers, rapists and thugs, people who do not hesitate to use violence on anyone they may meet. We are familiar with recent examples of criminals escaping from prison to commit heinous crimes in order to get transportation, food or money or just to "get back" at the society which put them behind bars.
Contrary to the contention of many people, these prison inmates are not just a bunch of mixed-up kids. They were put in prison after being convicted of crimes, often crimes of violence; they were incarcerated only after exhausting all the many avenues open to them under our judicial system. The most disturbing aspects is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his appointees in the penitentiary service insist on discussing the situation merely on the basis of reform, rehabilitation and parole. This makes about as much sense as a speech by Jackie Onassis on poverty.
The fact is that it is ridiculous talking about reforming a prisoner unless he makes himself available to be reformed. It has almost reached the point at which a prisoner in a Canadian jail simply will not wait around unless he happens to like it there. If he likes the food and is free to kick the guards and other prisoners around, and if he can run the prison the way he wants it run, then he just might hang around for a while. This is not good enough. Before we undertake to do anything by way of reform or rehabilitation we must ensure that when a lawbreaker is sen-

tenced to jail he is kept there for the duration of his sentence. As it is now, and as it has been for too long, the prisoner is the sole object of the government's sympathy.
Too often we hear of riots in our prisons and we hear afterward that many of the guards are tried or disciplined for being too rough with the inmates. We hear how tough it is for prison inmates, but we ignore the complaints of prison staff-that their lot is even rougher than that of the inmates. I would like to point out to my colleagues in the House that we must not lay the blame for what is going on at the feet of the present Solicitor General. He has not been in that position long enough to be able to get a full count of how many prisoners are at large. When he took over his post there were almost as many convicts outside as inside our jails. Anyone who was sentenced to prison under the previous Solicitor General knew that he would not have to stay in prison unless he really wanted to do so. There were many avenues open to him. If he wanted to go to Spain, for instance, he knew that he would be able to get a passport and be allowed to leave the country. If he just wanted to go into town and take a job, he could get help either from inside or outside the prison.
In short, Mr. Speaker, when the present Solicitor General took over his office the prison system was in a shambles. Under the previous Solicitor General we saw a breakdown of the Bail Reform Act. We saw a complete breakdown of the parole system. We saw instances where convicted rapists were allowed weekend passes from prison to commit still more crimes of rape, undoubtedly feeling that they would never be suspected of crimes while they were serving a sentence. The simple fact is that they were not serving terms, at least not in the accepted sense of serving a term. What is to be gained in having a court try a suspect at great expense, find him guilty and then sentence him to prison, only to have him released on his own recognizance as though he were a soldier on a weekend pass? What can we possibly gain from a system that permits a suspected bank robber to be free on bail, or without bail, and which allows him to commit crimes in order to raise the price of a good defence lawyer? This has happened, as the hon. members here know only too well.
Adding to the confusion we have the justice minister placing the blame for this mess in one quarter, the Solicitor General blaming someone or something else, the courts and judges placing the blame on the laws, and finally the police blaming the whole system. There is an old saying that applies to the military, and it also applies to high political office. It goes something like this: "The chief can delegate authority, but he cannot delegate responsibility". The person who is in charge of the show must be prepared to accept responsibility for it, whether it is a success or a flop. In the case of the penitentiaries system, the parole system and the bail system, the present Solicitor General deserves some measure of sympathy for the mere fact that he has agreed to accept responsibility for the mess they are in, and he has at least admitted that things are not as they should be. He has called for an investigation, possibly because of the pressure brought to bear on his office from the official opposition, and he deserves our support in such an investigation.

I do not envy the Solicitor General, Mr. Speaker. The former Solicitor General had an uncanny talent for creating confusion and for laying to waste the best laid plans of mice and men. Some of the appointments he made while in that office are clear evidence of his inability to choose the best man for the job, and unfortunately some of those appointments will give the present Solicitor General some sleepless nights. If and when the full scale investigation of the penitentiaries system is undertaken, I hope that it will extend into the area of political appointments to important posts in the system. Some of the jobs handed out to political hangers-on are jobs that call for a large degree of expertise in the prison administration, and I think that the investigation should include the appointment of a former post office employee to the post of commissioner of the penitentiary service. There were excellent people near the top level of the service who had spent their entire working lives in the service. It would have made a great deal more sense to look in their direction for a commissioner when the appointment was made. I cannot help feeling that some of the problems we are experiencing with the penitentiaries system start at the very top of the administration.
While I can commiserate with the new Solicitor General, and I might even sympathize with him. I must say I am disturbed by his statement that he is satisfied with the 18 per cent failure rate in the operation of the parole system. I am afraid that I cannot feel comfortable with a minister who admits that he is satisfied with failure. I would have preferred to have him say to this House that he would not be satisfied until he had achieved zero failure rate in the parole system, and while this is not likely to happen, at least it is a more worthy objective than the acceptance of an 18 per cent failure rate. As it is now, we do not know what sort of objective he has in mind, and it is important at this point for us to at least have some idea as to what he hopes to achieve, and what steps he proposes to take in order to accomplish his objective. His suggestion that a study of the whole situation is needed is a good start. It would be difficult for any of us to suggest at this point what remedial action should be taken to bring some order back to the system-the penitentiaries, parole, and all of the other aspects of the correctional system.
But, Mr. Speaker, the first step is obvious to all of us. Convicted lawbreakers have been sentenced to prisons in our country, and they were sent there so they would be separated from the rest of society. The first step must be to take whatever steps are required to ensure that they are kept in those institutions. While I will not argue the point that our prisons are overcrowded, that is not a valid reason for allowing prison inmates to walk the streets of our cities while we are working out the solutions to the problems.
If inmates are getting help from prison employees in making escapes, these people must be rooted out. If more guards and other personnel are needed, then they must be hired. But these people must be hired on the basis of their suitability for the job, rather than for their political persuasion or favours to the party in the past. I do not think that this is a really serious problem. What I do believe is that there is a serious breakdown in the prison service at or near the top of the administration. When that is cleared up, we will find, I am quite certain, that the other prob-

May 15, 1973
Penitentiaries
lems can be cleared up in short order. Until the day when the rank and file employees in the penitentiaries system come to believe in the competence of their superiors, right up to the top of the system, we will be faced with a morale problem. As long as we have such a serious morale problem among the guards and correctional officers, we will have riots, protests, prison breaks, and general disorder throughout the system.
Let us stop blaming the guards for the shape the prisons are in, and let us stop directing all of our sympathy towards those people who have been sentenced to prison. Our whole perspective is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is time for us to make it clear to the inmates of our prisons that that is just what they are, and that they are going to have to earn everything that they receive in the way of consideration. Our primary job is to protect the innocent from the guilty, not the other way round.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a certain amount of sympathy for the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). He has inherited a problem created by his predecessor as a result of a policy of permissiveness advocated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the former members of his cabinet. The matter has now come to a head like a boil on the back of the neck of the Solicitor General. We live in a supposedly civilized country. A civilized country is one in which its citizens, the average man and woman on the street, you and I, Mr. Speaker, can live without fear of violence. People are concerned about their own safety and they are concerned about the safety of their families and their friends. They read almost daily in the press, they see and hear on television and hear on the radio of persons granted bail committing further crimes. They hear of escapes from prisons of dangerous criminals, or they hear of persons who have been convicted of serious crimes being allowed out shortly after committal, either on a daily pass to work or to attend university or in some cases to attend hockey games. I find it very difficult to explain to a law-abiding constituent who has sacrificed to send his children to university why someone who has broken the law, can, while in jail, at the expense of the state, attend a university and obtain a degree. In some cases, these people end up with a government job.
I feel we have the wrong perspective. The intellectuals, psychiatrists and some politicians, for some reason or another, are of the opinion that if someone commits a crime he or she is not to blame, but that society is to blame. Who makes up society except you and I, the man on the street, the person doing his best to equip himself in our society, raise his family and be a good citizen? We are told that we are at fault. I suggest that is a very ridiculous theory. If a child misbehaves in class at school, do you pat him on the head and say he is not at fault, then punish the rest of the class? I am not suggesting that we should not concern ourselves with rehabilitation, but rehabilitation is a very complex matter. We must first look at the purposes of our laws and the penalties provided. The protection of society must be the first and foremost consideration. This is more important to me than rehabilitation, and it must be given first priority.

The second consideration is punishment. In this enlightened day, because of our educational system and the media, I believe all persons in Canadian society know what is right and what is wrong and when they are breaking the law. They are also aware of the consequences of breaking the law. Punishment should be a real thing; it must be an effective deterrent. There is no deterrent and no punishment when a person, upon being sent to jail, is treated in a better manner and receives more benefits from the state than many of our hard-working low income citizens.
Rehabilitation is vital. I have practised law for some 23 years during which time, I have acted as defence counsel for many people, so I appreciate the importance of rehabilitation. However, rehabilitation is important only in the cases of persons who are capable of being rehabilitated. These persons must be assisted to return to this society and take their proper places as citizens of this great country. I suggest that those persons who are not capable of rehabilitation must be handled in such a manner that they are not a danger to society, either through escape or being allowed out on weekend passes. They must endure their punishment.
The inquiry we expect the parliamentary committee to carry out must be a thorough and searching one; an inquiry which will result in a re-examination of our present system of bail, parole and passes. It should be an inquiry which will result in a reorganization of our present system in order that the public will once again feel secure and have the confidence in and respect for our judicial system which they had not too many years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of saying a few words in connection with this motion to refer this very important matter to a standing committee of this House. I know this is a very agonizing matter for the government and the Solicitor General in view of what has transpired in the last few days and, indeed, what has transpired over the last few years. However, the people of this country are not looking to the Solicitor General, the judicial authority, the police or the courts alone for a remedy to the situation. They are looking to this parliament for the necessary laws and recommendations to ensure that every Canadian is guaranteed the protection he expects in a country which cherishes the values we cherish in Canada.
Others have listed their qualifications in speaking on this motion. I want to assure hon. members who are not aware of the fact that I have perhaps the unique experience of having been not only a defence counsel and a Crown attorney, but of having served for some 15 years as a magistrate and a judge of the juvenile court. I know the problems involved in providing an adequate system of justice.
First of all, I think it is necessary that we put the whole matter in perspective and realize that we are talking here of only those who have been committed to one of the penitentiaries for which the federal government is responsible. We are not talking about the majority of people sentenced to jail to serve their time in provincial institutions. While I know the federal government, through the
May 15, 1973

Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), is responsible for the enforcement of criminal laws in this country, it is only the federal responsibility for penitentiaries we are dealing with here.
The number of people we are talking about is very minimal in relation to the total population and, indeed, in relation to the total number of people who run afoul of the law from time to time. It has always been emphasized by every court of law in this country that in sentencing an individual who has been convicted of any offence there are three basic principles to be considered. First of all, and I say foremost in any court with which I am familiar, the first principle is protection of society. The second principle is the deterrent effect, any sentence might have upon others who might be inclined to run the risk of committing a similar crime. The last principle, and perhaps this is important from the point of view of society, and one which seems to have got out of balance, is rehabilitation of the convicted person.
The problem is, of course, how to reconcile the interest of protecting society from criminals who have committed serious offences with the necessity and interest of society in rehabilitating those persons. I am sure that anyone who has had any experience with the law knows that people who are to be found in penitentiaries in this country are not people who are victims of some momentary transgression. In almost every case I know of where a penitentiary term has been imposed, it has been imposed on a person who has had many scrapes with the law, and in every case it has been a very serious breach of the law that gave rise to that penalty.

The problem then becomes one of the penitentiary service, and we are dealing of course with the administration of that service and the program they must have in order to do the job. The important part of the program is the rehabilitation of the convicted person. We have heard many stories of escapes from institutions and many accounts of the inadequacy of the facilities therein, and comments have been made by many people on the type of institution that we must have to adequately house convicted persons to ensure that they will no longer be a menace to society. In order to do this we must take into account the fact that adequate staff is required and, what is perhaps more important, a number of people with training, knowledge and the necessary qualifications.
The matter of how much money society and parliament are prepared to allocate to the penitentiary service for the rehabilitation of prisoners has always been a difficult problem. Because of this there has always been a lack of facilities of all kinds. I submit to the House that this is one of the reasons we are having the difficulties that we have been hearing and reading about in the last few days.
I submit that if this committee is to function properly and carry out the responsibility which we are giving it, it will be necessary for it to look into the type of facilities that are required in order to adequately house prisoners. Whether these institutions are maximum security institutions or any other type, they must be adequate and they must be staffed by properly trained and qualified people.

Since, as someone said earlier in this debate, most of the prisoners will eventually return to society, there must be an adequate program to ensure that they are rehabilitated whenever possible. With this goes a system of identification and encouragement for those who can be rehabilitated. The responsibility for this situation is not entirely that of the courts of this country, nor is it entirely that of the penitentiary staffs; it is the responsibility of this government and of all members of the House to see that the necessary remedies are found and the necessary action taken to put those remedies into effect.
I welcome the opportunity to discuss this urgent and important problem which affects the confidence of all Canadians in the ability of our system of justice to protect society as a whole.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is now Wednesday morning. We started out this debate on Tuesday shortly after two o'clock. I am sure the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) will agree with me that it was not long after 2 p.m. that he started having to field questions on a very difficult and unfortunate situation that has developed within the Canadian penitentiary service. I think the fact that we are still here on another day indicates the seriousness that Members of Parliament place on the situation that has developed within the Canadian penitentiary service, and I hope some of the things that I will say in the next 15 or 20 minutes will be of some value and benefit to the Solicitor General in the role he is endeavouring to fill in that office.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggests I make it short, and another hon. member suggested I should sit down. I say to the hon. member who suggested that I sit down that if he paid more attention to what is going on in parliament and stood up more often, perhaps this institution would be better off and the people of Canada would be better off. He happens to be picking up $28,000 a year for being here, and he should be producing some words in this institution that would be of value in solving some of the problems that this nation is facing.
I am standing here at this late hour to try to contribute in solving one of the chronic problems facing this nation in relation to the Canadian penitentiary service and the way in which it is being operated at present. First of all, I say to the Solicitor General, as I have said publicly before this debate, that I think he has adopted the type of approach to the problems related to the penitentiary serv-
3806

May 15, 1973
Pen i ten tiaries
ice that we should have adopted a long time ago. I think the Solicitor General, in the approach he has taken in moving across this country and speaking, not just to the wardens of institutions but to the correctional officers and the inmates, is adopting the right kind of approach and in the end I think he will be successful in solving the problems facing the country as a result of the erosion of the system.
I think that is the only way to solve the problem. I would say that his candid and cogent comments in relation to the escapes that have occurred indicate a very real appreciation of the problems with which he is confronted. I believe that the minister is sincere in the task he has accepted and has tried to undertake it in the best possible way, but I believe also that he has some real problems within the Canadian penitentiary service. At the same time, I am fearful that he might be made a scapegoat for the incompetence that is involved in the way these penitentiaries are being operated at present.
I had a long association with the Canadian Penitentiary Service even before there was a solicitor general's department that administered it. At that time it was under the Department of Justice. I was pleased to see the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) here. For many years he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of justice and worked very closely with me, as did the minister of justice, in the establishment of the first minimum security institution at Springhill and the present-day medium security institution which exists in that town.
It would only be fair at this time to say that the warden, or whatever you might call him now that they have fancy names for people who work in these institutions, of Springhill and the warden of the maximum security institution at Dorchester have done an outstanding job from the point of view of penology and protecting the people who are employed in those institutions and the inmates. I think they performed yeomen service in seeing the lid was kept on, especially at Dorchester. Mr. Bennett, who operates the institution at Dorchester, is a phenomenal person who has had to cope with unbelievable problems from an overcrowding point of view, problems which the Solicitor General, who visited that institution a short time ago and was asked questions about it in the House today, admits are unbelievable from every point of view, overcrowding, personnel, problems associated with inmates and the types of cliques which developed in that institution, and which the Solicitor General in his own way has tried to alleviate. These problems are real. They are real at Dorchester, they are real at Springhill and at every other penal institution. They are real because there has been a breakdown in the penal system.
In carrying out the kinds of inquiries that have been suggested we might assist the Solicitor General in solving some of the problems he faces. Every possible consideration should be given to the undertaking of the studies that have been suggested. I am not a member of the standing committee, but I feel it has tried to do an honest job in producing information for the public and for the Solicitor General by questioning the witnesses who appeared before it. That committee has indicated that it feels a
special committee should be established. The Solicitor General indicates that he believes there should be a judicial inquiry. I think it would not be a bad idea if both were undertaken at the same time so that there could be a correlation of the two types of information produced to see if the same conclusions are reached, and if the same conclusions are reached then the Solicitor General will know where to go from there.
More than that, I believe the Solicitor General has been badly let down by people in the public service who are supposed to be serving him. They have put him into most embarrassing situations in this House and throughout the country because of what has happened at a number of institutions. I say to him that although he is dedicated and sincere, he must also show to members of this House and to the public generally that he is tough, that he is willing to make heads roll when they should roll. And I say that heads must roll so far as the Canadian penitentiary service is concerned because of the kinds of things that have been happening in institutions all across the country.
I do not believe that there is any other answer. The top echelon of the penitentiary service must be cleaned out, fast, before we discover that there are more inmates running around outside than there are in the institutions and before we discover that most of the police forces in Canada are spending more of their time tracking down escaped inmates than in performing their other obligations to the Canadian people. For instance, Mr. Speaker, while I did not say anything about it, I was very upset over the fact that three inmates escaped from Dorchester penitentiary with a gun. Where that gun came from, I do not know. How many other guns there are in Dorchester penitentiary, I do not know. But these three hardened criminals, who had bad records, got out and kidnapped two people. They held them captive for a period of time until the RCMP recaptured them and returned them to the institution.
That is a very dangerous sort of situation to develop in any community. It developed as the result of a gun being smuggled into the penitentiary. Such a situation is very frightening for people in my constituency because there is an institution in it, and Dorchester happens to be only about 15 miles away from my home town, Amherst. When inmates escape from there, they pose a real threat; and when those kinds of inmates escape from Dorchester or St. Vincent de Paul, anything can happen. Particularly, anything can happen when we have the kind of laws we have in Canada today, when no man dies no matter what he does, no matter what crime he commits. There is no such thing as capital punishment, so that a murderer who escapes from prison has nothing to lose. He can kill as many people as he wishes. The most that will happen to him is that he will be returned to prison for whatever time the government and the Parole Board determine is the correct time for him to be there. This is one of the reasons why I have indicated that I will support the retention of capital punishment as strongly as I can. There is only way to deal with a murderer who escapes from an institution; he must know that if he commits another murder he is going to the gallows and that will be the end of his life.
My opinion is that the Solicitor General is trying as hard as he knows how to get some sense back into the

May 15, 1973

penitentiary service. Again I say that many of the people serving under him are doing a disservice to him because they are not nearly as willing as he is to put common sense back into the service. The Solicitor General must get rid of these people, and fast. He must get common sense back into the penitentiary service and into our whole approach to penology. I also say to him that if he does not show that kind of toughness, then no matter how dedicated he may be, he will not be long in that job because the Canadian people want common sense put back into the service. We want to know that when a man is sent to an institution, the government will be responsible for keeping him there for whatever time is required until a rehabilitation program indicates that he is ready to return to society.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF SECURITY OF PENITENTIARIES, PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have any intention of becoming involved in this debate but I think it only right that I place a few points on the record because I believe that the motion the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) has brought before the House is of extreme importance. The recent incident at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary has sparked us all into action, action which was called for prior to the last general election when people were concerned about law and order and respect for the law.
Society has been concerned for a considerable length of time. The repetition of jail breaks has left society questioning the administration of the penal services, questioning parole, questioning temporary leave and questioning the role of the custodial officer. We have to arrive at a happy balance in this matter, Mr. Speaker, because the penal service which was here yesterday is here today and will be here tomorrow. The question is how we can develop such a system to the point that we will have the necessary confidence in it and to see that it receives the proper funding. The committee has an awesome responsibility. I hope they will travel across the country and visit the penitentiaries to discuss matters with the administrators, the custodial officers and the inmates. Unless they do, the results will not be satisfactory.
I am one who believes that you cannot rehabilitate all those who are sent to the penitentiary, but at the same time I am one who believes that in our advanced form of life those who are sent there are deserving of the opportunity, regardless of how depraved they may be, of becoming rehabilitated. What we have to be concerned about is when a person reaches the stage that rehabilitation is no longer a reality; then we must be extremely concerned and take all precautions that are required.
The minister's neck is on the block. The minister must come up with the proper answers because society demands protection. When we talk about society and the inmate, it is the interest of society, the protection of society, that must be borne in mind. We cannot get away from that. I get very disturbed when I read that prisoners are eating steak when we on the outside, the fortunate ones, are eating hot dogs. We must arrive at a proper balance, but it must be weighted in favour of society.
When we talk about rehabilitation some people would say "dig a hole, put them in there and forget about them".
Peni ten tiaries
What concerns me about that, Mr. Speaker, is that at the end of their term they come out to face society not rehabilitated, and perhaps even more vicious and violent than when they went in. What we have to think about are the alternatives. Do we just put them in jail and forget about them or, in a pragmatic and realistic way, say that during their term in jail they must undergo some program of rehabilitation? I think we must accept the latter view because if we do not, we have been debased and dehumanized. We would be doing a disservice to those we would like to be rehabilitated and to the public which I believe is interested in a reasonable form of rehabilitation.
As I said, we must be concerned about the protection of society. I am an abolitionist because I am concerned about the morality of capital punishment and about the fact that a mistake can be made. I am not convinced that capital punishment is a deterrent. We must be concerned about a proper penal service being established and administered in order that the protection of society shall remain paramount.
The committee has an awesome job. It is expected to solve this age-old problem and have answers within the next couple of months. Whether they can do that or whether the judicial inquiry that the minister has asked for is the better way, I am not sure and I do not think it matters which way it is done. All I know is that at this particular time we are saved by the fact that some chaps are jumping the wall has captured the imagination of Canadians.
I trust and hope that, as a result of this motion, the wisdom of the members who will form the committee will enable them to assess and investigate the situation. Perhaps after due deliberation they will be able to come back with recommendations that will not only satisfy society but that will also satisfy the inmates. We have seen what has happened in the United States; when an inmate is placed in a cell like a dog, he will bark and bite as a dog. The responsibility of this committee is enormous but I have every confidence that it will make the necessary recommendations which the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) can implement in order to make our penal service one of the best in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to add a number of comments to the debate on the motion before us. As a result of the deep concern that I, and the constituents I represent, feel, we believe that only by means of a public outcry can our confusion be heard. Apparently this is the only manner in which to move the government into a position where it will tackle and solve certain problems. Old standards are being violated but society today wants us to return to basic standards of behaviour and those who break the law will have to be punished accordingly.
Some people wonder why inmates are given privileges which very often are not available to those in the lower economic groups of our society. They look with disbelief when inmates are given hockey tickets and then escape from the game. If I may mention a case in Winnipeg, the Manitoba government paid approximately half a million dollars for hockey tickets to the games of the professional Winnipeg Jets. These were given to many deserving groups, and I do not quarrel with that, but they were also given to various prison societies. The tickets were then

given to inmates and we had escapes from the Winnipeg arena as well.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF SECURITY OF PENITENTIARIES, PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCES
speechtext: That was punishment.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF SECURITY OF PENITENTIARIES, PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCES
speechtext:
Watching the Winnipeg Jets was hardly a punishment, Mr. Speaker, though it might be with some other hockey teams! People also question why certain inmates can attend university at public expense. I am not saying this is entirely wrong, but we had a case in our area where an escapee, after stealing property, damaging it and forcing the owner to pay the cost of the damage, was able to attend university and laugh at the rest of us. They question the attitudes which allow this type of rehabilitation system.
I believe our attitude toward crime has, at best, become permissive. Unfortunately, today in our society a person is responsible to no one. It is a basic attitude for too many of our people that one is responsible only to himself. The attitude is: I can do as I please. As long as I do not hurt the other fellow too much, I can do what I please and no one has any business telling me not to do it.
That type of society is one in which I do not want to live. Society has an obligation to teach its young persons basic principles and to expect the middle-aged and old to obey its laws; otherwise, society breaks down and crime increases. We in this country have prided ourselves, perhaps falsely, on the fact that our crime rate is not that of our neighbour to the south, and our cities are safer than those to the south. That may have been the case in the past. Let us not fall into the trap of permissiveness, so that our urban centers will remain the places of safety they have been until now.
The role of prisons is twofold. One is to isolate prisoners from society. Men and women who have broken the law of this country and have been convicted through due process of law have a penalty to pay. If society is to survive, that penalty must be paid. The safety of society through isolating those who insist on breaking the law must be the underlying criterion of imprisonment. We must not lose sight of the fact that incarceration is for the protection of the majority; it is not simply punishment of those who have committed a crime.
Second is the question of rehabilitation. We have now been told that it is not rehabilitation but a reintegration process. This recognition of the need of rehabilitation for members of society is a mark of a civilized society. It is only a civilized society obeying civilized, humane laws which can or will recognize that people who break those laws must be rehabilitated back into the society they forcibly left. Despite the aspects of this society in which we live, the hallmark of our society must be just and equitable laws for the continued well-being of the majority. These laws are not simply for retribution; they are not there for the creation of a police state or for the creation of fear or hatred.
We as individual citizens must subscribe to the laws of this country. If not, we must be punished. While we must be cognizant of the ills in the society in which we live, we cannot allow our attitude to be soft, or one of soft-pedalling those who commit crimes. It might be argued that you

cannot legislate morality. You might even take that argument to the nth degree and say that possibly we do not need any laws. The law is there to provide a standard to which all citizens must subscribe. If citizens do not subscribe to that standard, punishment must be invoked. I believe that punishment is a deterrent, not only to the person against being a repeater but to all of us.
Another point that was mentioned today by various speakers was that of Christian principles. In the society in which we live, Christian principles very clearly teach humanity and the value of the individual. Christian principles and the basic view of the value of the individual gave recognition to and became the underlying principle of many of our laws today. While these Christian principles teach the value of the individual, reconciliation and the re-establishment of brotherly love, they also very clearly teach that justice is part and parcel of the Christian principle in a Christian society.
You cannot have justice without punishment. A person who takes it upon himself to break the law of society must pay the penality which society deems necessary for the crime committed. The rehabilitation concept is one of value. However, I believe that a percentage of the inmates who are incarcerated in our federal penitentiaries have made a mockery of the rehabilitation system. They are the ones who have taken advantages of special passes, weekend passes, temporary passes and any other kind of pass that may be devised from one day to the next. They have often broken parole by committing heinous crimes during the period of parole. These hardcore criminals should be dealth with severly; the maximum penalty that the law provides should be imposed.
Society today is questioning the guidelines governing our rehabilitation system. I wish to cite an example of what happened in a provincial jail at Headingley, Manitoba. The Manitoba government hired an ex-inmate who was to work with the inmates and potential employers as inmates were approaching the time when they would be back in society. The guards in that jail protested the hiring of this ex-inmate. The minister of health and social development for the province, in defending this ex-inmate, said that the man had qualifications. He said the man was qualified because he "had gone the whole route". What an apprenticeship program for that particular job!
In order to return to the rationale of protecting society and providing rehabilitation within the restrictions that must be imposed if society must still be protected, it cannot be said that all persons who are advocating rehabilitation are bleeding hearts. They are moved by the massive number of human lives that have been wrecked by crime. We see young men who have made wrong decisions at a very early age and have embarked upon a road leading to crime and imprisonment. I am sure every member is aware of the tremendous price many of these people pay and the price society has to pay in lost ability and potential.
I suggest to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) that we strengthen our rehabilitation program. Personally, I believe that prison chaplains have made a great contribution in our prisons. I would like to see an increase, not only in funds for but in the role of prison chaplains. We must keep in mind that justice can only be served if
May 15, 1973

penalties are imposed and we insist that they be paid by those who break the laws of society.
I subscribe to the establishment of a special committee as the Solicitor General sees fit, that we proceed to strengthen the law and that we fulfil the trust society has given to us. However, it must be an orderly society. Where heads should roll, let them roll. As this clean-up proceeds, the Solicitor General will have our support and I am sure he will earn the gratitude of all Canadian citizens.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak for very long. I agree with almost everything that has been said by members on both sides of this House. I extend my sympathies to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) because he is in a very difficult position. I was told when I first came to the House of Commons in early January that the job of the Solicitor General was one of the most onerous in the cabinet. I hope the committee, when it is set up, will be composed of people with wide-ranging interests, because with all due respect to the profession of law, lawyers do have limitations.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF SECURITY OF PENITENTIARIES, PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE OF SECURITY OF PENITENTIARIES, PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCES
speechtext:
I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald). She said the investigation should be wide-ranging and indicated that the whole subject of equality in sentencing should be looked at closely. I have for many years read a lot of newspapers and something I read seven or eight years ago struck me as being very odd. A report appeared in a Saskatchewan paper about prison sentences meted out in the province. One individual who had embezzled $12,000 from a bank received a suspended sentence of two years while another who forged a cheque for $75 got a six month jail sentence. Both of these crimes were first offences. Maybe there were differing circumstances but the disparity struck me then as being peculiar. I had noticed many similar anomalies in the intervening years.
There is a great deal of mistrust of our whole system of justice because of the existence of crime and dishonesty in high places. To the south, we find a government which ran an election campaign on the platform of law and order, but which is itself breaking the law. We must remember that a man becomes a prisoner only if he is caught and convicted. Many offenders are never caught or convicted. They still live in our midst.
I have been a school principal for many years and I have dealt with all kinds of youngsters. In the last 23 years I have noticed a great deal of change in our youth. Youth is becoming extremely cynical about the way in which the laws of our nation are enforced, because different standards seem to be applied to different people. When these cynical people reach our prisons, there are problems.
The enforcers of the laws are themselves sometimes its transgressors. Many a time I have had a young person in my office who would say: Mr. Nesdoly, I did not stop at a stop sign; I was stopped and ordered to pay a $25 fine. I said, all right, you broke the law, so you pay it. Then, he said: You know there is a policeman down Main Street who makes a U-turn in the middle of the street; that is against the law, but he can do it; he was not chasing
Penitentiaries
criminals, or anything. Or a local magistrate can park his car on the wrong side of the street without any attention being paid to it. These things have been brought to my attention too many times for them not to contain some elements of truth.
I believe the committee should look at the high proportion of our prison population represented by Indian and Metis people. It seems to me there is a disproportionate number of them in our prisons. Why are they there, and what sort of rehabilitation program is being carried on to help them?
Perhaps we should be considering, too, the question of the location of prisons. Why do they need to be so close to cities? Why not farther north? Some people say they must be close to services. We must remember that Australia was colonized by convicts. So was Siberia.

speechtext:
I hope so, too, Mr. Speaker. This has been a long debate, an exhausting debate, a debate which could have been avoided had the motion made yesterday under Standing Order 43 been accepted.
One thing I want to mention before I discuss the mechanics of the committee, which is the purpose of my rising, is that I have listened carefully throughout the debate to members from both sides discussing the various aspects of the motion, but no one has yet mentioned the demoralizing effect which the bail reform law and the ease with which escapes are made from our penal institutions has had on law enforcement agencies. Premature parole and the operations of the bail reform legislation are seriously impeding the work of law enforcement agencies and seriously affecting the morale of those agencies throughout the country.
With respect to the committee itself, the reason a select committee of the House was suggested yesterday under Standing Order 43, and today in the standing committee, and by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) was primarily because of these two factors: first, the workload which now lies on the plate of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and, second, the need for acting with haste in connection with this inquiry. The standing committee will not have finished its examination of the estimates of the Solicitor General's department until the end of the month. It will then embark upon consideration of the wiretapping legislation which has been referred to it. Judging from the interest shown in this legislation during the second reading stage in the House, its consideration will certainly take at least until the third week of June.
The committee which will be authorized by the House to study the matters embodied in the resolution before us

May 15, 1973
Peni ten tiaries
must act much more rapidly, so it will be my intention to try to convince the steering committee that a sub-committee of the standing committee be struck, composed, perhaps, of three members from this side of the House and three members from the other side of the House together with one member from the New Democratic party and one member from the Social Credit party. This committee would be small enough to act with flexibility and the degree of haste necessary. I would suggest that it set about its work visiting the institutions which are causing the most chronic problems as well as those which might be described by some in the Solicitor General's department as being models for penal institutions.
In order to set up a subcommittee to accomplish that sort of task it may well be, and likely will be, that the standing committee will have to be enlarged by eight additional members. I understand that discussions have taken place among the House leaders, and the government would not resist an enlarged Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs should the committee make that recommendation to the House. I hope it will do so as its very next meeting, and that necessary steps are taken to enlarge the committee by eight members, or by whatever number the committee deems advisable, thus permitting the subcommittee to be formed and to set about its work at once.
The need for rapid action is demonstrated by all who have participated in this debate and by the events that have occurred. I will not discuss the merits here because I hope to be a member of that subcommittee, if the suggestion is adopted, and there will be plenty of time to make my comments at that stage. Certainly I do not want to flog the Solicitor General any more tonight. We are compassionate people on this side of the House and in my view he has been flogged sufficiently today to draw emphatically to his attention the very deep-rooted dissatisfaction, not only of members of opposition parties but members of his own party, with the manner in which the penitentiary system is functioning.	[DOT]
In addition, there have been comments relating to the bail reform legislation, the parole system and the temporary leave of absence program which must convince the Solicitor General that there is a great deal to be desired. We were promised some kind of action by his predecessor well over a year ago with respect to the bail reform legislation, but we have not had action. Neither have we had action with respect to the penal system.
Not all ill winds blow no good, and perhaps the events of the day have had one advantageous effect, at any rate, and that is to focus public attention on this question and to bring Parliament to the point where it finally takes action. It is my hope and the hope of those on this side of the House that we agree to set up a small subcommittee which will have the flexibility and rapidity of movement to enable an early report to be made to the House, hopefully a report that will not be ignored, one containing recommendations that will be accepted by the government and which will go a long way toward curing the problems confronting the Solicitor General's department.
